items.prompt: Available moves have positive sizes. dp(s) counts the number of move sequences whose total is exactly target, starting from current sum s. What should dp(target) equal?
constraints: Reaching target completes one valid sequence.
No additional moves are needed after completion.

options.text: target, because the base value should match the target sum.
1, because the empty continuation completes the already valid sequence.
0, because there are zero moves left to make.

feedback.reason: At an exactly completed state, the empty continuation is one valid way, so a predecessor path reaching this state contributes one to the count.

blocks.text: A predecessor transition adds the number of completions from its successor. If dp(target) were zero, every valid path ending at target would contribute nothing and all counts would collapse to zero. Setting it to one represents the single choice to stop successfully. This is a semantic base case, independent of whether the recurrence is memoized or tabulated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: The state counts valid continuations, not remaining actions. The empty continuation is one valid way to finish.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target: The numeric target is not a count of continuations; the base must follow the state meaning.

items.prompt: All item weights are positive. A recursion count(i, remaining) counts subsets of items i onward whose weights sum exactly to remaining. Which base rules are correct?
constraints: Items may be used at most once.
A remaining value below zero is invalid.

options.text: If remaining == 0, return 1; if i == n while remaining > 0, return 0; if remaining < 0, return 0.
If remaining == 0, return 1; if i == n, return 1 for every remaining value; if remaining < 0, return 0.
If remaining == 0, return 0; if i == n while remaining > 0, return 0; if remaining < 0, return 0.

feedback.reason: Successful completion, exhausted choices, and invalid overshoot are distinct terminal states with different counts.

blocks.text: remaining == 0 means the target has been met, so the empty choice over the rest is one valid completion. Reaching i == n with a positive remainder cannot complete the target, and a negative remainder is already invalid. The index alone cannot determine the base result because the resource component changes whether the terminal state is successful.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_only_success: Exhausting items succeeds only when the target is also satisfied; positive remaining means the construction is incomplete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_remaining_failure: Zero remaining is the exact target condition and represents one completed subset, regardless of unused items.

items.prompt: A suffix recurrence has top-down base solve(n) = 0 because no cost remains after the last element. What is the corresponding bottom-up initialization?
constraints: dp(i) stores the same suffix cost as solve(i).
The table has entries 0 through n.

options.text: Set dp[0] = 0 because bottom-up always starts at index 0.
Do not initialize any base because the loop will infer it.
Set dp[n] = 0 before filling earlier states.

feedback.reason: The empty suffix is state n in both implementations, so its value remains zero even though evaluation direction changes.

blocks.text: Top-down reaches n through recursive calls; bottom-up stores the same state explicitly and starts from it. Moving the seed to index 0 would change what the value represents. Memoization and tabulation can differ in overhead and reachable states, but they must agree on every state value, including bases.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dp_zero_zero: The base location follows the state meaning. dp[0] represents the full suffix, not the empty suffix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.omit_base: The first computed state reads the terminal value; without a defined seed it consumes an undefined or default value.

items.prompt: Order the bottom-up setup for a suffix recurrence whose states depend on larger indices.
constraints: For i < n, dp[i] reads dp[i + 1] and possibly dp[i + 2].

elements.text: Allocate entries including every terminal index the recurrence may read.
Process nonterminal indices in dependency-safe order.
Read the state representing the original problem.

feedback.reason: The transition cannot safely consume a terminal state until that state exists and has its semantic base value.

blocks.text: A consumer may run only after its terminal states are valid

items: Allocate every state the recurrence can read, including terminal indices such as n.
Write each terminal value from the state meaning instead of relying on a language default.
Process nonterminal states in an order where their larger-index dependencies are already initialized or computed.
Read the state that represents the original input only after all states it depends on are valid.

blocks.text: Allocation creates storage, not mathematical meaning. Iterating before explicit base initialization can silently propagate a default value that is valid for neither counting nor optimization.

blocks.title: Initialization order
blocks.text: Allocate → seed semantic bases → evaluate dependents → read the original-problem state.

items.prompt: A recurrence uses dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2] with dp[0] = 1 and dp[1] = 1. Which compressed initialization is correct before computing i = 2?

options.text: prev2 = 1 and prev1 = 0 because dp[1] has not been iterated yet.
prev2 = 1 and prev1 = 1.
prev2 = 0 and prev1 = 1 because index 0 means no work.

feedback.reason: The two live variables must start with the exact values of dp[0] and dp[1].

blocks.text: Compression changes storage, not base semantics. At i = 2, the recurrence expects the values of both terminally initialized predecessors. A default zero for either variable produces a different sequence even though the update formula is unchanged. The same rule applies to rolling rows: every boundary cell required by the first interior update must already represent its logical DP state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_one: dp[0] is one valid empty construction under the stated recurrence, so replacing it with zero changes every later value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_zero: dp[1] is an explicit base, not a state waiting for the general loop; it must be seeded before i = 2 reads it.

items.prompt: dp(i) is the minimum deletion cost for suffix s[i:], with dp(n) = 0. What should an implementation return when s is empty?

options.text: Return dp[0] = dp[n] = 0.
Reject the input because the transition needs at least one character.
Return 1 to count the empty suffix as one deletion.

feedback.reason: With n = 0, the requested state is exactly the terminal empty-suffix state whose cost is zero.

blocks.text: The state meaning determines both the base value and whether the general loop is entered. Empty input is not an exceptional unknown case; it is the terminal suffix by definition. Confusing counting and cost bases can produce a plausible but wrong one. Always test the original input against terminal-state conditions before assuming at least one transition will run.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.error: The original state is already the defined terminal state; no transition is necessary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one: The state is a cost, not a count of constructions. The empty suffix incurs zero deletion cost.

items.prompt: A grid path counter normally sets dp[0][0] = 1. The start cell is blocked. What initialization is correct?
constraints: A path may visit only unblocked cells.
The answer counts paths from the start to the destination.

options.text: Keep dp[0][0] = 1 because every grid has one empty path at its origin.
Leave dp[0][0] uninitialized and start at its neighbors.
Set dp[0][0] = 0, so no path can propagate from an illegal start.

feedback.reason: The origin seed represents one valid way to occupy the start, which does not exist when the start is blocked.

blocks.text: Initialization encodes feasibility as well as recurrence identity. In an open grid, one path of length zero starts at the origin and seeds later counts. A blocked origin is not a legal state, so its count is zero and every reachable count remains zero. The same boundary check applies to blocked destinations or other base states that are valid only under stated constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_origin: The empty path is not valid when the starting state itself violates the cell constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_origin: Neighbors must receive path counts from valid predecessors; an undefined origin risks propagating a default inconsistent with the blocked condition.

items.prompt: A minimization DP combines feasible costs with impossible branches. Which initialization prevents an impossible branch from winning as zero cost?

options.text: Represent impossible states with a sufficiently large infinity sentinel and exclude or guard it before arithmetic.
Initialize every impossible state to zero so it is easy to add.
Use negative infinity for minimization because it marks a state as unavailable.
Use whichever branch is evaluated first as the default even when it is impossible.

feedback.reason: Minimization must not treat an unavailable route as a free route; the sentinel must lose to every feasible finite cost.

blocks.text: Zero is a valid cost and would incorrectly attract a minimum. Positive infinity represents no feasible solution, but adding to it must be guarded or implemented with a safe sentinel so it does not overflow. Negative infinity would always win a minimum and therefore has the opposite meaning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_impossible: Zero is a feasible cost in many problems and would create a false cheap path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_infinity: Negative infinity is smaller than every feasible cost, so it incorrectly wins minimization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_branch_default: Evaluation order cannot turn an impossible branch into a valid candidate.

items.prompt: A DP counts valid ways to construct an empty target from available moves. Which base value follows the combinatorial identity?

options.text: Set the empty-target state to 1: choose no moves, which is one valid sequence.
Set it to 0 because no move was selected.
Set it to -1 so the first move can increment it to zero.
Set it to the number of available move types.

feedback.reason: The empty construction is the multiplicative identity for extending counted sequences: exactly one sequence uses no moves.

blocks.text: A transition that appends a legal move needs a valid predecessor count. The empty target has one construction—the empty sequence—so a one-step move can contribute one way to its destination. Setting it to zero erases all sequences whose final move lands exactly on the target.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_empty_way: No moves is still one valid empty sequence in a counting recurrence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_one: Counts do not need a compensating negative base and it would corrupt every extension.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_count: The number of move types does not describe the number of ways to construct an empty target.

items.prompt: In a grid path-count DP, a blocked destination cell is encountered after reachable neighbors have been computed. What value should its state receive?

options.text: Zero, because no legal path may enter or leave the blocked cell.
One, because every cell has one trivial path before neighbors are considered.
The neighbor sum regardless of blocked status.
Keep any value written before the obstacle was discovered.

feedback.reason: Blocked cells are unreachable under the problem's movement contract, so their count must be the additive zero.

blocks.text: The obstacle check is part of initialization and every cell transition. A blocked destination cannot receive paths from its neighbors, and treating it as one or retaining stale data would create routes through the obstacle. The same rule applies whether the cell is the origin, an interior state, or the destination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_blocked: A blocked cell has no legal empty path unless the problem explicitly defines otherwise.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_neighbors: Neighbor paths cannot enter a blocked cell.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_previous: A stale value would represent paths that the current obstacle contract forbids.

items.prompt: What base value represents zero ways to build an impossible state in a counting DP?

options.text: 0, because no valid construction reaches that state.
1, because every state has one implicit construction.
-1, because impossible always means a negative count.
Infinity, because impossibility is a large optimum.

feedback.reason: Counting DP uses zero as the additive identity for an impossible number of constructions.

blocks.text: Do not reuse this base for optimization or minimum-cost DP without checking that problem's identity and sentinel contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_way: One is the empty-construction identity in some counting bases, not an impossible state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_one: Negative counts are not the usual count sentinel.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.infinity: Infinity is an optimization sentinel, not a count.

items.prompt: What must a minimum-cost DP use for an unreachable state?

options.text: A sentinel larger than any valid cost, handled so it is not arithmetically mistaken for a reachable path.
Zero, because no path has no cost.
One, regardless of transition costs.
Negative infinity, because the state is unavailable.

feedback.reason: The optimization identity must not allow an unreachable candidate to win a minimum comparison.

blocks.text: Guard additions from overflowing or turning infinity into a finite value. The sentinel must be compatible with the transition and output contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero_cost: Zero can incorrectly beat every reachable positive path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_cost: A fixed one is not a universal unreachable cost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_infinity: Negative infinity would incorrectly win a minimum.

items.prompt: In a grid-path DP, why is the origin base case initialized before filling later cells?

options.text: It seeds the recurrence so paths entering adjacent cells have a valid predecessor contribution.
It sorts rows and columns before transitions.
It marks the origin unreachable so no path can begin.
It removes all boundary checks from later cells.

feedback.reason: A path recurrence needs a valid source state from which neighboring paths accumulate.

blocks.text: The origin's value depends on whether the task counts paths, minimizes cost, or maximizes reward. The key is that it is initialized before consumers read it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_grid: Grid order is not created by base initialization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.block_origin: Blocking the origin removes every path that starts there.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_edges: Boundary cells still need valid transition guards.

items.prompt: What defect occurs if a DP table cell is read before its base or predecessor state is initialized?

options.text: An uninitialized value can propagate into later states and corrupt the recurrence.
The table becomes asymptotically faster because initialization is skipped.
The table is sorted automatically by the first read.
Every language supplies the mathematically correct DP identity automatically.

feedback.reason: DP transitions consume stored semantics; an uninitialized entry is not a valid identity or sentinel by default.

blocks.text: Initialize all required base and unreachable states before iterating, or make the recursion explicitly branch on an uncomputed marker.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.faster_fill: Skipping required state changes correctness, not asymptotic class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_table: Reads do not sort table entries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_effect: Default memory values rarely match the problem's DP contract.
